personas.persona: Sets the firm's posture and owns the judgments it will not delegate: which engagements to take, how to scope them, and how far a claim can be pushed before it stops being true. She signs engagement letters in a plain, careful register and is the one who insists an overview describe the firm's work as representative rather than complete. Her prose is unhurried and exact; she would rather a sentence say less and hold than say more and wobble.

Owns client relationships at the executive level and frames how an engagement is presented from kickoff through close. He writes status reports that lead with the decision at hand and leave the supporting detail to an appendix, and he is comfortable telling a client something they did not want to hear. His voice is direct and a little dry, built for a room of operators rather than a boardroom.

Runs engagements day to day, turning a partner's scope into a workplan and keeping the client's team moving. She writes the kickoff memos and chairs the working sessions, and her minutes read like someone who was actually in the room, capturing what was decided and who owns the next step. Her tone is warm but organized, and she is the one who reconciles what a client asked for with what the data will actually support.

Manages a workstream end to end and is the hinge between the analysts building the model and the client who has to live with the answer. He writes tight status updates and the running email threads about data requests, plain and unfussy, and he chases a late data pull without making it a confrontation. His memos are short and structured, never dressed up beyond what the point requires.

Carries the analytical core of an engagement, translating messy client data into the operating-model or cost picture the team can defend. She drafts the substance of deliverables and is meticulous about what a number can and cannot be made to say. Her writing is careful and lightly hedged, the register of someone who has watched a confident chart fall apart under one good question.

Does the hands-on analysis a workstream runs on, cleaning data and building the exhibits that end up in a status pack or a deck. Practical and quick, she writes plainly and keeps her notes close to the evidence, flagging an assumption rather than burying it. She is comfortable in the weeds and prefers a caveated answer to a tidy one that will not hold.

Builds and maintains the engagement's models and the exhibits that feed status reports and briefing decks. Precise and methodical, he writes to the workpaper rather than the reader, annotating sources so a conclusion can be traced back through the file. His prose is spare and neutral, and he would rather label something uncertain than let it read as settled.

A senior analyst who owns the benchmarking and the data-heavy sections of a deliverable, at home in a spreadsheet the way others are in a memo. She writes compactly and lets the exhibit carry the argument, keeping her own commentary to what the data will support. Her register is even and unshowy, shaped by a firm that treats an overstated finding as a liability.

An entry-level analyst learning the firm's habits, doing the first pass on data and drafting the raw material a manager will shape. Eager and literal, he over-documents rather than under-documents and confirms an instruction before he runs with it. His writing is still finding its register, plainer and more tentative than a senior hand's, but pinned closely to the evidence.

Runs the firm's internal machinery on the commercial side: engagement administration, billing arrangements, and the terms that sit behind an engagement letter. He writes to be unambiguous rather than to be read, and his notes are brisk, procedural, and pinned to a specific day. He treats a loose contract detail as the kind of thing you close out quietly before it ever reaches a client.

Owns resourcing and scheduling for the practice, matching people to engagements and untangling the collisions that follow. Methodical and low-drama, he writes short functional notes that say exactly who is doing what and by when. He would rather have a staffing plan confirmed in writing than agreed in a hallway, and he keeps the calendar honest.

Manages an engagement's workstreams and keeps the cadence of status reports and working sessions on schedule. Organized and calm under a deadline, she writes crisp minutes and updates that separate what is decided from what is still open. Her voice is businesslike and readable, and she is quick to convert a loose discussion into a dated list of owners and next steps.

A consultant who does the analytical legwork on a workstream, from data cleanup to the exhibits behind a finding. Diligent and grounded, she keeps her working notes tied to their sources and would rather flag a soft spot in the analysis than gloss over it. Her writing is plain and functional, closer to a well-annotated worksheet than to polished prose.

Does the background research that grounds an engagement: market scans, company profiles, and the source-gathering that feeds a briefing deck. She is organized and citation-minded, and her handoffs come with the source attached so a manager never has to ask where a figure came from. Her writing is plain and orderly, closer to a well-kept file than to prose.

Runs benchmarking and comparables, assembling the outside reference points a team measures a client against. Careful and a little skeptical, he distrusts a clean number until he has seen how it was built, and he says so in his notes. He writes compactly and neutrally, more interested in whether a figure holds than in how it reads.

Handles data pulls and the first cut of analysis, turning raw client extracts into something a consultant can work with. Quick and practical, he documents his steps as he goes so a number can be reproduced, and he flags a gap in the data rather than papering over it. His notes are terse and matter-of-fact, written for the next person in the chain.

Focuses on industry and competitive research, the desk work behind a situation assessment. Curious and thorough, she reads widely and distills what she finds into short, sourced summaries a manager can lift straight into a memo. Her voice is clear and unhurried, and she is careful to mark where the evidence thins out.

Supports the deck-building side of an engagement, turning analysis into exhibits and keeping a status pack consistent from page to page. Detail-obsessed about labels, footnotes, and sources, she catches the mislabeled axis everyone else skims past. She writes briefly and functionally, and treats an unsourced chart as an unfinished one.

Gathers and organizes the source material an engagement runs on, from public filings to the notes taken in a working session. Steady and reliable, she keeps the shared record in order so nobody rebuilds work that already exists. Her writing is plain and economical, the register of someone documenting for a team rather than performing for a reader.

Works the quantitative side: data cleaning, reconciliation, and the arithmetic that has to tie before a finding is trusted. Patient and exacting, he chases a reconciliation until it closes and notes the assumptions he had to make to get there. His prose is spare and technical, written to the workpaper and rarely dressed up.

Does primary research and interview support, drafting the question guides and writing up the notes from client conversations. Attentive and even-handed, he captures what was said without editorializing and separates a fact from an impression. His write-ups are clean and readable, and he is careful not to let a single quote stand in for a pattern.

Assembles the market and company research that frames an engagement's early weeks. Fast and resourceful, he can turn a thin brief into a usable profile quickly, and he is upfront about where he had to reach. He writes in short, direct paragraphs, sourced but never fussy, built to be handed up and reworked.

Handles data collection and the comparison sets a team leans on, keeping sources labeled and methods repeatable. Systematic and unflappable, she would rather flag a shaky comparable than let it slide into a deck. Her notes are compact and neutral, written for a colleague who will need to check them.

Supports the research desk across engagements, from source-gathering to fact-checking a draft before it goes out. Meticulous and quietly thorough, she is the one who catches the stale figure or the claim that overreaches what the data shows. Her writing is plain and careful, and she is more comfortable adding a caveat than removing one.

Focuses on data collection and the early analysis behind an operating-model or cost review. Practical and steady, he keeps his work close to the source and documents his steps so a manager can follow the trail. His notes are brief and unadorned, written to move work forward rather than to impress.
